newsitem.title: USA: Clinton inspects tornado damage in Arkansas.
newsitem.headline: Clinton inspects tornado damage in Arkansas.

text.p: President Bill Clinton had an unpleasant homecoming on Tuesday as he surveyed the debris-strewn path of a chain of deadly tornadoes that swept through Arkansas last weekend, leaving 25 dead and hundreds injured.

Clinton, the Democratic governor of this southwestern state for 12 years before his election as president, flew to this devastated college town from Little Rock by helicopter after arriving aboard his Air Force One jetliner in the state capital, where he started his political career.

He saw a view from the air that looked like a war zone, with houses crushed, trees ripped from the ground and twisted at crazy angles and roofs of buildings blown away. Swollen muddy creeks striped a normally placid countryside of pine trees and pastureland.
The cloudless sky gave little hint of the nightmarish windstorms that howled through the area last Saturday.

Arkadelphia, about 50 miles (80 km) southwest of Little Rock with a population of about 10,000 people, was literally ripped apart by winds that exceeded 200 mph (320 kph) as the deadly twisters cut a 250-mile (400 km) swath from south Arkansas to the state's border with Missouri.

Once on the ground, Clinton walked through the town's main square, a tableau of shattered buildings, splintered pieces of lumber and broken glass. A sign identified one destroyed restaurant as "Shaw's Garden and the Garden Tea Room," but all that remained were the brick columns that once adorned the building.

In casual clothes and surrounded by a small army of leading Arkansans including Republican Gov. Mike Huckabee, Clinton stopped frequently to chat with local residents and reminisce about his visits to the town as a boy.
"It's obvious that you all have done a lot of work in just a couple of days. That's Arkadelphia," he said, looking at bulldozers that were hard at work cleaning up the damage.
Clinton acted swiftly to speed federal financial assistance to victims of the disaster, issuing a declaration on Sunday that made nine Arkansas countries eligible for disaster relief.
The White House said government funds would help provide temporary housing, reimburse victims for uninsured property losses and help individuals and businesses rebuild.
It said local governments could receive federal funds on a cost-sharing basis for debris removal, emergency policing and other needs.

As he toured the scenes of devastation in his home state, Clinton also acted to make federal disaster assistance available to residents of Ohio and Kentucky, which were hit by storms that caused heavy flooding.

Clinton has made swift federal disaster relief assistance one of the hallmarks of his presidency, and since entering the White House in 1993 he has visited the scene of every major U.S. natural catastrophe to console victims and help restore morale.
But he said his emergency visit to his home state, which also included a damage assessment in the poor, predominantly black Little Rock suburb of College Station, was "profoundly different."
"It is different when you know the people and know the location," the president said. "I spent a large part of my life in this little community that was blown away."
